## Teaching points

1. A severe headache that the patient describes as different from his usual migraines is a red flag; a migraine history does not lower the risk.
2. The Ottawa SAH rule rules out SAH only when every criterion is absent: age 40 or older alone means further testing is needed.
3. A negative CT is reassuring only within 6 h of a clearly timed onset. Here the headache had begun the previous evening, during exertion, so the CT was done outside that window.
4. Do not call a bloody tap traumatic just because xanthochromia is absent: it can take up to 12 h to form and visual inspection is insensitive. High CSF red cell counts after a sudden headache need vascular imaging.
5. Sentinel headaches precede aneurysmal SAH in a substantial minority of patients (10–43% in the studies cited by this report) and may be the last chance to secure the aneurysm before it ruptures.
